steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing block shuffle and rotation (BSR), an input transformation attack that improves the transferability of adversarial examples. Cover DNN vulnerability, white-box vs black-box attacks, existing transferability methods and their attention heatmap issue, our method, and a contributions list.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown superior performance in many tasks, for example image classification, segmentation, object detection, face recognition, and others. But even with these achievements, DNNs have been found to be very vulnerable to adversarial examples, which look very much like legitimate examples but can deliberately misguide deep learning models into making unreasonable predictions. These vulnerabilities raise serious concerns, especially in security-sensitive applications like autonomous driving and face verification.

Adversarial attacks can in general be put into two types, white-box attacks and black-box attacks. In white-box attacks the attacker has complete access to the architecture and parameters of the target model. Black-box attacks on the other hand only have limited information about the target model, so they are more applicable for real-world applications. In the white-box setting, some studies use the gradient with respect to the input sample to generate adversarial examples. These crafted adversarial examples show transferability across neural models, which means adversarial examples generated on one model can fool not only the victim model but also other models, and this makes them suitable for black-box attacks. However, existing attack methods have outstanding white-box attack performance but their transferability is relatively poorer, and this limits how well they can attack real-world applications.

Recently, several approaches have come out to improve adversarial transferability. These include adding momentum into gradient-based attacks, attacking multiple models at the same time, transforming the image before calculating the gradient, using victim model features, and modifying the forward or backward process. Among them, input transformation based methods, which modify the input image for the gradient calculation, have been shown to be very effective at improving transferability. However, we find that all the existing input transformation based attacks lead to different attention heatmaps on different models. This difference in the attention heatmaps could limit how far the adversarial transferability can go.

The attention heatmaps show the crucial regions for classification. Because of this, we want to keep the attention heatmaps of adversarial examples consistent across different models. We only have access to one white-box model for the attack, so first we look at ways to disrupt the attention heatmaps. As shown in Fig. 1, if we randomly shuffle the divided blocks of the image, we can disrupt the intrinsic relation inside the image, and this leads to different attention heatmaps than the raw image. Based on this, we propose a novel input transformation based attack called block shuffle and rotation (BSR). It optimizes the adversarial perturbation on several transformed images to eliminate the variance among the attention heatmaps on various models. Specifically, BSR randomly divides the image into several blocks, and then the blocks are shuffled and rotated to make new images for the gradient calculation. BSR uses the average gradient on several transformed images, to eliminate the variance of the random transformation and to stabilize the optimization.

Our contributions are as follows:

- We show that breaking the intrinsic relation of the image can disrupt the attention heatmaps of the deep model.

- We propose a new attack called block shuffle and rotation (BSR), which is the first input transformation based attack that disrupts attention heatmaps for better transferability.

- Empirical evaluations on the ImageNet dataset show that BSR has much better transferability than the state-of-the-art input transformation based attacks.

- BSR is compatible with other transfer-based attacks and they can be integrated with each other to boost the adversarial transferability further.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown superior performance in many tasks, for example image classification [1,2], segmentation [3], object detection [4,5], face recognition [6], and others. But even with these achievements, DNNs have been found to be very vulnerable to adversarial examples [7,8,9], which look very much like legitimate examples but can deliberately misguide deep learning models into making unreasonable predictions. These vulnerabilities raise serious concerns, especially in security-sensitive applications like autonomous driving [10] and face verification [11].

Adversarial attacks can in general be put into two types, white-box attacks and black-box attacks. In white-box attacks the attacker has complete access to the architecture and parameters of the target model. Black-box attacks on the other hand only have limited information about the target model, so they are more applicable for real-world applications. In the white-box setting, some studies use the gradient with respect to the input sample to generate adversarial examples [8]. These crafted adversarial examples show transferability across neural models [12], which means adversarial examples generated on one model can fool not only the victim model but also other models, and this makes them suitable for black-box attacks. However, existing attack methods [13,14] have outstanding white-box attack performance but their transferability is relatively poorer, and this limits how well they can attack real-world applications.

Recently, several approaches have come out to improve adversarial transferability. These include adding momentum into gradient-based attacks [15,16], attacking multiple models at the same time [17], transforming the image before calculating the gradient [18,19], using victim model features [20], and modifying the forward or backward process [21,22]. Among them, input transformation based methods, which modify the input image for the gradient calculation, have been shown to be very effective at improving transferability. However, we find that all the existing input transformation based attacks lead to different attention heatmaps [23] on different models. This difference in the attention heatmaps could limit how far the adversarial transferability can go.

The attention heatmaps show the crucial regions for classification. Because of this, we want to keep the attention heatmaps of adversarial examples consistent across different models. We only have access to one white-box model for the attack, so first we look at ways to disrupt the attention heatmaps. As shown in Fig. 1, if we randomly shuffle the divided blocks of the image, we can disrupt the intrinsic relation inside the image, and this leads to different attention heatmaps than the raw image. Based on this, we propose a novel input transformation based attack called block shuffle and rotation (BSR). It optimizes the adversarial perturbation on several transformed images to eliminate the variance among the attention heatmaps on various models. Specifically, BSR randomly divides the image into several blocks, and then the blocks are shuffled and rotated to make new images for the gradient calculation. BSR uses the average gradient on several transformed images, to eliminate the variance of the random transformation and to stabilize the optimization.

Our contributions are as follows:

- We show that breaking the intrinsic relation of the image can disrupt the attention heatmaps of the deep model.

- We propose a new attack called block shuffle and rotation (BSR), which is the first input transformation based attack that disrupts attention heatmaps for better transferability.

- Empirical evaluations on the ImageNet dataset show that BSR has much better transferability than the state-of-the-art input transformation based attacks.

- BSR is compatible with other transfer-based attacks and they can be integrated with each other to boost the adversarial transferability further.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have established superior performance in many tasks, such as image classification [1,2], segmentation [3], object detection [4,5], face recognition [6], among others. Despite these achievements, DNNs have been observed to be significantly vulnerable to adversarial examples [7,8,9], which closely resemble legitimate examples yet can deliberately misguide deep learning models into producing unreasonable predictions. Such vulnerabilities raise serious concerns, particularly in security-sensitive applications such as autonomous driving [10] and face verification [11].

Adversarial attacks can generally be categorized into two types: white-box attacks and black-box attacks. White-box attacks have complete access to the target model’s architecture and parameters. In contrast, black-box attacks only have limited information about the target model, which makes them more applicable for real-world applications. In the white-box setting, some studies employ the gradient with respect to the input sample to generate adversarial examples [8]. These crafted adversarial examples exhibit transferability across neural models [12], i.e., adversarial examples generated on one model can deceive not only the victim model but also other models, making them suitable for black-box attacks. However, existing attack methods [13,14] demonstrate outstanding white-box attack performance but relatively poorer transferability, which limits their efficacy in attacking real-world applications.

Recently, several approaches have emerged to enhance adversarial transferability, including incorporating momentum into gradient-based attacks [15,16], attacking multiple models simultaneously [17], transforming the image before gradient calculation [18,19], leveraging victim model features [20], and modifying the forward or backward process [21,22]. Among these, input transformation based methods, which modify the input image for gradient calculation, have proven significantly effective in improving transferability. However, we find that all existing input transformation based attacks result in different attention heatmaps [23] on different models, and this discrepancy could limit the extent of adversarial transferability.

The attention heatmaps highlight the crucial regions for classification. Motivated by this, we aim to keep the attention heatmaps of adversarial examples consistent across different models. Since we only have access to a single white-box model for the attack, we first explore methods to disrupt the attention heatmaps. As shown in Fig. 1, randomly shuffling the divided blocks of the image disrupts the intrinsic relation within the image, leading to different attention heatmaps compared with the raw image. Based on this finding, we propose a novel input transformation based attack, called block shuffle and rotation (BSR), which optimizes the adversarial perturbation on several transformed images to eliminate the variance among the attention heatmaps on various models. In particular, BSR randomly divides the image into several blocks, which are then shuffled and rotated to create new images for gradient calculation. To eliminate the variance of the random transformation and stabilize the optimization, BSR uses the average gradient on several transformed images.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- We show that breaking the intrinsic relation of the image can disrupt the attention heatmaps of the deep model.

- We propose a new attack called block shuffle and rotation (BSR), the first input transformation based attack that disrupts attention heatmaps for better transferability.

- Empirical evaluations on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that BSR achieves much better transferability than the state-of-the-art input transformation based attacks.

- BSR is compatible with other transfer-based attacks, and they can be integrated to further boost adversarial transferability.
